visuals.title: Three depths of SSI
visuals.text: Most common organism at every depth: Staphylococcus aureus.

visuals.title: Working it up
nodes: Ultrasound or CT if deep or organ/space

visuals.title: Emergency approach
nodes: Antibiotics if cellulitis, pus or systemic
Open, wash out, debride necrotic tissue
Surgical review, back to theatre if deep

visuals.title: How the wound gets infected
nodes: Contamination: skin or gut flora, or outside sources
Staph aureus most common (lives on skin)

visual.caption: Superficial and deep SSIs stay in the wall. Organ/space SSIs sit in the space opened at surgery: abscess and sepsis risk.

visuals.title: Why necrotising infection is an emergency
nodes: Group A Strep or polymicrobial infection

events.x: Highest contamination risk; bacterial load kept down
Fewer SSIs in clean-contaminated and contaminated cases

glossary.Subcutaneous tissue: The fatty layer lying just beneath the skin.
glossary.Fascia: A sheet of tough connective tissue wrapping muscles and organs.
glossary.Intra-abdominal abscess: A pocket of pus inside the abdomen, for example after bowel surgery.
glossary.Orthopaedic: Relating to surgery on bones and joints.
glossary.Immunosuppression: A weakened immune system, from drugs such as steroids or chemotherapy, or from disease.
glossary.Emergency surgery: An unplanned operation done urgently, with less time to optimise the patient.
glossary.Malaise: A general feeling of being unwell, tired and uncomfortable.
glossary.Inflammatory markers: Blood tests such as CRP and white cell count that rise with infection or inflammation.
glossary.Tenderness: Pain when the area is pressed during examination.
glossary.Discharge: Fluid leaking from the wound; may be serous, bloody or purulent.
glossary.Pus: Thick fluid of dead white cells, bacteria and tissue debris.
glossary.Wound breakdown: Separation or failure of a healing wound, often due to infection.
glossary.Systemic toxicity: Whole-body illness from infection: fever, tachycardia, hypotension, confusion.
glossary.Tachycardia: A heart rate above 100 beats per minute.
glossary.Pain out of proportion: Pain much worse than the visible signs suggest; a classic warning of necrotising infection.
glossary.Spreading erythema: Redness that extends further over hours, showing infection is advancing.
glossary.Ultrasound: Imaging using sound waves; quick and good for finding superficial collections.
glossary.CT: Computed tomography: cross-sectional X-ray imaging, good for deep and intra-abdominal collections.
glossary.Imaging: Scans such as ultrasound or CT used to look inside the body.
glossary.Penicillin allergy: An allergic reaction to penicillins, which rules out flucloxacillin.
glossary.Theatre: The operating theatre; return to theatre means another operation.
glossary.Re-suturing: Stitching a wound closed again after it has opened.
glossary.Surgical review: Assessment by the surgical team to decide whether further operation is needed.
glossary.Escalate: Seek senior or specialist help because the patient is not improving or is seriously ill.
glossary.Flora: The normal bacteria living on the skin or in the gut.
glossary.Tissue perfusion: Blood flow through tissues, which brings oxygen and immune cells.
glossary.Immune response: The body's defence reaction against infection.
glossary.Monomicrobial: Caused by a single species of organism.
glossary.Bacterial load: The number of bacteria present in a site.
glossary.Incision: The surgical cut through the skin.
glossary.Tissue planes: Natural layers between tissues along which infection can spread quickly.
glossary.Surgical emergency: A condition needing an operation within hours to save life or limb.
glossary.Diabetes: Raised blood glucose that impairs white cell function and wound healing.
glossary.Obesity: Excess body fat; reduces blood supply to wounds and increases tension on closure.
